items.readable_text:
Content:
If a particle moves with constant velocity [MATH: \mathbf{u},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the position of the particle when [MATH: t=0] (i.e., the initial position).

Content:
Notice that the term [MATH: \mathbf u t] on the right-hand has units of [MATH: \textrm{speed} \cdot \textrm{time},] so we can think of this formula as being analogous to [MATH: \textrm{distance} = \textrm{speed} \cdot \textrm{time}.]

Content:
Suppose a particle moves with a constant velocity of [MATH: (3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s},] and its initial position is [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m}.] A sketch of this situation is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/52fc7ac6de3d9d30f226b172db02606b]

Content:
Let's calculate the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] seconds. In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf u = 3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}.]

Content:
Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \: \textrm{s}] is

Content:
[MATH: r|= r_{0} + ut; = (i + 2j) + (3i + 2j)(2); = (i + 2j) + (6i + 4j); = (7i + 6j)m.]

Content:
So, the particle is located at the point [MATH: (7,6)] after [MATH: 2] seconds, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1f3c66b389ede7599a37f02b11d4991c]

Content:
Notice the distance covered by the particle equals [MATH: 2 |\mathbf{u}|] because the particle is translated by the vector [MATH: \mathbf u] every second for two seconds.

sections.normalized_html: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}) \: \textrm{mi}] with a constant velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{mi/h}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] hours.
sections.readable_text: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}) \: \textrm{mi}] with a constant velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{mi/h}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] hours.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If a particle moves with constant velocity [MATH: \mathbf{u},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using [MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t,] where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle.

In our case, we have [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}, \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \: \textrm{h}] is [MATH: r|= r_{0} + ut; = (3j − i) + (i − j)(2); = (− i + 3j) + (2i − 2j); = (i + j)mi.]

A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}) \: \textrm{mi}] with a constant velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{mi/h}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] hours.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If a particle moves with constant velocity [MATH: \mathbf{u},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t,]
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle.

In our case, we have
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}, \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \: \textrm{h}] is
[MATH: r|= r_{0} + ut; = (3j − i) + (i − j)(2); = (− i + 3j) + (2i − 2j); = (i + j)mi.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that when a particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration [MATH: a] and initial velocity [MATH: u,] we can calculate its displacement [MATH: s] at time [MATH: t] using the formula

Content:
[MATH: s = ut + \dfrac12 a t^2.]

Content:
There is an analogous formula that works for planar motion. If a particle moves with constant acceleration [MATH: \mathbf{a},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t + \dfrac12 \mathbf{a} t^2,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is its initial velocity.

Content:
For example, suppose a particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m}] with acceleration of [MATH: (-\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})\,\textrm{m/s}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (3\mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s}.] What will be the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] seconds?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/274f9cc6a9fb3cc14dd2486087337295]

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 2\mathbf i + 2\mathbf j, \qquad \mathbf u = 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = -\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}.]

Content:
Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \, \textrm{s}] is

Content:
[MATH: r|= (2i + 2j) + (3i + j)(2) + (1)/(2)(− i + j)(2)^{2}; = (2i + 2j) + (6i + 2j) + 2(− i + j); = (2i + 2j) + (6i + 2j) + (− 2i + 2j); = (6i + 6j)m.]

Content:
So, the particle is located at the point [MATH: (6,6)] after [MATH: 2] seconds, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e14cf2317e70d7ba0ea94ef43badeb0d]

Content:
Watch out! The trajectory (path) of a particle that moves with nonzero acceleration in the plane is not necessarily a straight line!

sections.normalized_html: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\,\textrm{cm}] with an acceleration of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{cm/min}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{cm/min}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 4] minutes.
sections.readable_text: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\,\textrm{cm}] with an acceleration of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{cm/min}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{cm/min}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 4] minutes.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration [MATH: \mathbf{a},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t + \dfrac12 \mathbf{a} t^2,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 4\mathbf i - \mathbf j , \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = \mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 4 \, \textrm{min}] is [MATH: r|= (4i − j) + (i + j)(4) + (1)/(2)(i + 3j)(4)^{2}; = (4i − j) + (4i + 4j) + 8(i + 3j); = (8i + 3j) + (8i + 24j); = (16i + 27j)cm.]

items.title: Calculating the Distance Between a Particle and the Origin

sections.normalized_html: A particle moves from the origin with an acceleration of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{cm/s}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (-\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{cm/s}.] Find the distance from the particle to the origin after [MATH: 6] seconds.
sections.readable_text: A particle moves from the origin with an acceleration of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{cm/s}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (-\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{cm/s}.] Find the distance from the particle to the origin after [MATH: 6] seconds.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration [MATH: \mathbf{a},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t + \dfrac12 \mathbf{a} t^2,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 0\mathbf i +0 \mathbf j , \qquad \mathbf u = -\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = \mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 6 \, \textrm{s}] is [MATH: r|= (0i + 0j) + (− i − 2j)(6) + (1)/(2)(i + j)(6)^{2}; = (− 6i − 12j) + 18(i + j); = (− 6i − 12j) + (18i + 18j); = (12i + 6j)cm.]

Finally, the distance from the particle to the origin at this time is

[MATH: |r||=|12i + 6j|; = sqrt(12^{2} + 6^{2}); = sqrt(144 + 36); = sqrt(180); = 6sqrt(5)cm.]

[MATH: r|= (0i + 0j) + (− i − 2j)(6) + (1)/(2)(i + j)(6)^{2}; = (− 6i − 12j) + 18(i + j); = (− 6i − 12j) + (18i + 18j); = (12i + 6j)cm.]

[MATH: |r||=|12i + 6j|; = sqrt(12^{2} + 6^{2}); = sqrt(144 + 36); = sqrt(180); = 6sqrt(5)cm.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If a particle moves with constant velocity [MATH: \mathbf{u},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the position of the particle when [MATH: t=0] (i.e., the initial position).

Content:
Notice that the term [MATH: \mathbf u t] on the right-hand has units of [MATH: \textrm{speed} \cdot \textrm{time},] so we can think of this formula as being analogous to [MATH: \textrm{distance} = \textrm{speed} \cdot \textrm{time}.]

Content:
Suppose a particle moves with a constant velocity of [MATH: (3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s},] and its initial position is [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m}.] A sketch of this situation is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/52fc7ac6de3d9d30f226b172db02606b]

Content:
Let's calculate the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] seconds. In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf u = 3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}.]

Content:
Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \: \textrm{s}] is

Content:
[MATH: r|= r_{0} + ut; = (i + 2j) + (3i + 2j)(2); = (i + 2j) + (6i + 4j); = (7i + 6j)m.]

Content:
So, the particle is located at the point [MATH: (7,6)] after [MATH: 2] seconds, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1f3c66b389ede7599a37f02b11d4991c]

Content:
Notice the distance covered by the particle equals [MATH: 2 |\mathbf{u}|] because the particle is translated by the vector [MATH: \mathbf u] every second for two seconds.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Position Vector of a Particle Moving With Constant Velocity

Example Prompt:
A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}) \: \textrm{mi}] with a constant velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{mi/h}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] hours.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If a particle moves with constant velocity [MATH: \mathbf{u},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t,]
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle.

In our case, we have
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{i}, \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \: \textrm{h}] is
[MATH: r|= r_{0} + ut; = (3j − i) + (i − j)(2); = (− i + 3j) + (2i − 2j); = (i + j)mi.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Particles Moving With Constant Acceleration

Content:
Recall that when a particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration [MATH: a] and initial velocity [MATH: u,] we can calculate its displacement [MATH: s] at time [MATH: t] using the formula

Content:
[MATH: s = ut + \dfrac12 a t^2.]

Content:
There is an analogous formula that works for planar motion. If a particle moves with constant acceleration [MATH: \mathbf{a},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t + \dfrac12 \mathbf{a} t^2,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is its initial velocity.

Content:
For example, suppose a particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m}] with acceleration of [MATH: (-\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})\,\textrm{m/s}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (3\mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s}.] What will be the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 2] seconds?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/274f9cc6a9fb3cc14dd2486087337295]

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 2\mathbf i + 2\mathbf j, \qquad \mathbf u = 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = -\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}.]

Content:
Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 2 \, \textrm{s}] is

Content:
[MATH: r|= (2i + 2j) + (3i + j)(2) + (1)/(2)(− i + j)(2)^{2}; = (2i + 2j) + (6i + 2j) + 2(− i + j); = (2i + 2j) + (6i + 2j) + (− 2i + 2j); = (6i + 6j)m.]

Content:
So, the particle is located at the point [MATH: (6,6)] after [MATH: 2] seconds, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e14cf2317e70d7ba0ea94ef43badeb0d]

Content:
Watch out! The trajectory (path) of a particle that moves with nonzero acceleration in the plane is not necessarily a straight line!

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Position Vector of a Particle Moving With Constant Acceleration

Example Prompt:
A particle starts moving from the point with position vector [MATH: (4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\,\textrm{cm}] with an acceleration of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{cm/min}^2] and an initial velocity of [MATH: (\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{cm/min}.] Find the position vector of the particle after [MATH: 4] minutes.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration [MATH: \mathbf{a},] the position vector of the particle at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u} t + \dfrac12 \mathbf{a} t^2,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{r}_0] is the initial position of the particle and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have
[MATH: \mathbf{r}_0 = 4\mathbf i - \mathbf j , \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} +\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = \mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}.]

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after [MATH: t = 4 \, \textrm{min}] is
[MATH: r|= (4i − j) + (i + j)(4) + (1)/(2)(i + 3j)(4)^{2}; = (4i − j) + (4i + 4j) + 8(i + 3j); = (8i + 3j) + (8i + 24j); = (16i + 27j)cm.]
